name: Kiribati
summary: 33 atolls straddling the equator and the date line, formerly the British Gilbert Islands; independent in 1979. Battle of Tarawa (1943).

knownFor.label: First to see the new year
knownFor.note: Its Line Islands are in the earliest time zone.

location.value: Central Pacific; about 810 km² spread over 3.5 million km² of ocean.

terrain.value: Low coral atolls rarely more than a few metres above sea level, in the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line groups; Banaba is a raised limestone island.

climate.value: Hot, humid tropical maritime climate; rain is heavier in the north, and the drier southern Gilberts often suffer droughts.

resources.value: Tuna and other fish in a vast ocean zone, coconuts for copra, and seaweed; Banaba’s phosphate was mined out by 1979.

disasters.value: Cyclones, droughts and rising sea levels.

population.value: About 130,000 people (2024 estimate), almost all I-Kiribati, with roughly half living on South Tarawa.

urbanisation.value: About half the people live on crowded South Tarawa, the capital area, where islets such as Betio are among the most densely settled in the Pacific.

disease.value: Diabetes and heart disease from imported food.

migration.value: Movement from the outer islands to South Tarawa; emigration to New Zealand through the Pacific Access Category, and seasonal work in Australia and New Zealand.

economicBase.value: Fishing licence fees from foreign tuna fleets, copra exports, remittances, foreign aid and income from the Revenue Equalisation Reserve Fund.

tradeRoutes.value: Food and fuel are imported by sea through Betio port on Tarawa; regular flights connect Tarawa and Kiritimati with Fiji.

wealth.value: A lower- or upper-middle-income economy, depending on aid and fishing licences.

moneyAndTax.value: The Australian dollar is the currency (Kiribati also issues its own coins); government income comes mostly from fishing licences rather than taxes.

inequality.value: Gap between the capital and outer islands.

governmentType.value: A republic whose president (Beretitenti) is head of both state and government, elected by voters from candidates nominated by parliament.

keyRulers.value: Led by elected presidents (Beretitenti); the first held office from independence in 1979 until 1991, and power has since changed hands through elections.

succession.value: Presidents are chosen in national elections from candidates nominated by parliament, and may serve no more than three four-year terms.

institutions.value: The Maneaba ni Maungatabu (a single-chamber parliament), an elected president and cabinet, the High Court and island councils.

stability.value: Stable since 1979, with regular elections and peaceful changes of government, though cabinets have occasionally fallen to no-confidence votes.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between loose parties and island-based groups in parliament, sometimes over foreign policy such as ties with Taiwan or China.

armyAndTech.value: Kiribati has no armed forces; the Kiribati Police Service keeps order, and Australia and New Zealand help with maritime patrols.

majorWars.value: No wars since independence; before it, US forces took Tarawa from Japan in the Battle of Tarawa (November 1943), one of the Pacific War’s bloodiest fights.

territoryChange.value: No changes since 1979; the Treaty of Tarawa (1979) ended US claims to the Phoenix and Line Islands, and the Ellice Islands (Tuvalu) had split off in 1975.

alliancesRivals.value: Switched recognition from Taiwan to China (2019).

inventions.value: Traditional navigation by stars and swells.

scienceEducation.value: University of the South Pacific campuses.

openness.value: Very open: most food, fuel and goods are imported, and the country depends on foreign fishing fleets, aid and work abroad.

communicationTransport.value: Small boats and inter-island ships link the atolls; Air Kiribati flies domestic routes, and causeways join the islets of South Tarawa.

religion.value: Mostly Christian: Roman Catholics are the largest group, followed by the Kiribati Uniting Church and other Protestants; the Bahá’í Faith also has followers.

languageWriting.value: Gilbertese (te taetae ni Kiribati), written in the Latin alphabet since missionary times in the 1800s, and English; both are official.

artsArchitecture.value: Dance with chanting, mats and fans woven from pandanus, and the maneaba, a large open meeting house with a steep thatched roof.

socialStructure.value: Extended families (kainga) and village communities, in which respected old men (unimwane) lead discussion in the maneaba.

sharedIdentity.value: An I-Kiribati identity built on the maneaba, the Gilbertese language, Christianity and life on the ocean, alongside a wider Pacific identity.

dailyLife.value: Families eat fish, coconut, breadfruit and babai (giant swamp taro), though imported rice and tinned food are now common.

neighbours.value: Tuvalu, Nauru and the Marshall Islands nearby, with Fiji, Tokelau and the US islands of Howland and Baker across the ocean.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity, brought by Protestant (from 1857) and Catholic (from 1888) missionaries, alongside customary respect for elders and the maneaba.

riseSignals.value: Independence from Britain on 12 July 1979, after self-government in 1977; the Gilbert Islands took the new name Kiribati.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; the country has stayed independent and stable since 1979 but faces the threat of rising seas.

declineSignals.value: Bought land in Fiji (2014) as insurance against rising seas.

outcome.value: Still an independent republic and a member of the Commonwealth (since 1979) and the United Nations (since 1999).

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
